docs.title: Capability and Ownership Matrix
docs.text: The Capability and Ownership Matrix helps analysts define capability data, compare maturity and ownership across audiences, and plan how responsibilities should evolve. The analyst user guide follows the work from gathering evidence through importing YAML, exploring the screens, recording decisions, and exporting the reviewed plan.

docs.title: Start with the analyst guide
docs.text:
The analyst user guide is the end-to-end manual for building and using a project matrix. It explains the planning lifecycle, how to collect and shape source data, how to use each screen, and how to export and reuse the capability document.

The YAML format reference defines the document structure, settings, capability fields, maturity values, dependencies, timeline dates, and runtime validation differences. Start with the reference when preparing an import file or checking a validation error.

docs.title: One shared planning context
docs.text:
The application provides three connected views for the same selected capability and audience. The Matrix supports comparison, the Capability journey explains one capability’s progression, and the Federated domain map shows dependencies and ownership boundaries.

flowchart LR
    C["Shared context<br/>Capability · Perspective<br/>Current · Focus"] --> M["Matrix"]
    C --> J["Capability journey"]
    C --> D["Federated domain map"]
    M <--> J
    J <--> D
    M <--> D

The Current period is the reference point and Focus is the comparison point; either may be in the past or future. YAML maturity values are anchored at settings.timeline.asOf and the final timeline period, with optional dated milestones between them.

docs.title: Data flow and scope
docs.text:
The versioned YAML document is the portable project data source. The browser preview holds changes in memory until export, while the Tauri desktop app validates and saves successful changes in its application data directory.

flowchart LR
    Y["Project YAML"] --> R["React application"]
    R --> V["Matrix · Journey · Domain map"]
    R --> I["Import and export"]
    R --> T["Tauri desktop shell"]
    T --> P["Python validation sidecar"]
    T --> S["App data capabilities.yaml"]
    R -. "proposed metadata only" .-> C["Content mapping review"]
    C -. "future integration" .-> X["CCMS delivery / PDF manuals"]

The application does not discover source data, publish to a CCMS, validate a production DITA configuration, or generate PDF manuals. The bundled capability document is illustrative; replace it with project-validated data before planning.

docs.title: Analyst user guide
docs.text:
This guide takes an analyst from the first planning question to a reviewed capability document and a planning decision in the Capability and Ownership Matrix. Its sequence follows Robert Horn’s information-mapping approach: concepts explain what something is, processes explain how work flows, procedures give actionable steps, structures show relationships, facts define values, examples demonstrate the data, and troubleshooting helps recover from errors. Each section is labeled by its principal information type so readers can find the kind of information they need.

The application is a planning and visualization tool, not an automated discovery service or an authoritative system of record. Analysts gather and reconcile the source information, prepare the YAML document, and use the application to compare perspectives, expose dependencies, and record proposed maturity and ownership decisions.

docs.title: 1. Planning lifecycle
docs.text:
Information type: Process. A capability matrix is most useful when it is treated as a lifecycle rather than as a one-time spreadsheet exercise. The analyst defines the decision to be made, gathers evidence, establishes a shared capability and maturity model, creates and validates the YAML document, loads it into the application, uses the linked views to plan, and exports a reviewed snapshot for the next planning cycle.

flowchart LR
    A["Frame the decision"] --> B["Gather and reconcile evidence"]
    B --> C["Define capabilities, levels, owners, and dependencies"]
    C --> D["Create capabilities.yaml"]
    D --> E["Validate and import"]
    E --> F["Explore Matrix, Journey, and Domain map"]
    F --> G["Record decisions and milestones"]
    G --> H["Export and review the YAML"]
    H -->|Next review cycle| B

Information type: Principle. The matrix should make a decision more defensible, not make uncertain evidence look precise. Keep observed facts, stakeholder judgments, assumptions, proposed targets, and unresolved questions distinguishable in the source notes and in capability summaries or decisions.

Information type: Procedure. Use the following lifecycle when starting a new project or refreshing an existing matrix.

  1. Frame the planning question. Write down the scope, the decision owner, the intended planning horizon, and the choices the matrix must support, such as which work belongs in a product and which service should be shared.
  2. Identify the evidence and participants. List relevant product documentation, service catalogs, architecture diagrams, operating procedures, road maps, support data, and subject-matter experts. The application does not collect these sources for you.
  3. Reconcile the evidence. Confirm capability names and boundaries with the people who deliver, use, fund, advise on, and govern the work. Record source, date, owner, confidence, and disagreement in your working notes so a maturity score can be traced to evidence.
  4. Define the model. Agree on capability IDs, capability descriptions, maturity-level names and descriptions, the meaning of ownership, dependency semantics, audience perspectives, and the timeline before assigning scores.
  5. Create the YAML. Start from the bundled example or the YAML format reference, then replace the illustrative sample with project-validated records.
  6. Validate and load the document. Check the structure and cross-references, then use Import YAML in the application. Correct validation errors in the YAML or editor before interpreting the views.
  7. Use the views to plan. Compare an audience’s needs in the Matrix, examine one capability’s path in the Journey, and test its dependencies and ownership boundary on the Domain map.
  8. Record and review decisions. Update the relevant capability, maturity levels, milestones, dependencies, owners, and settings. Have the appropriate stakeholders challenge the assumptions and proposed handoffs.
  9. Export the reviewed data. Use Export YAML to create a portable snapshot, check it into the project’s approved document store, and use that version as the starting point for the next review.

Information type: Principle. The order of these activities matters because a view cannot correct a poorly bounded capability or an unsupported score. Agree on definitions and provenance before using the visualization to make a recommendation.

docs.title: Define the decision and scope
docs.text:
Information type: Concept. A capability is a stable description of an ability that a product, service, team, or wider domain must provide. It is not necessarily a feature, project, team, or system; define it at the level needed to discuss maturity, ownership, and dependencies without tying its identity to one implementation.

Information type: Procedure. Draft each capability by naming the outcome or ability, stating its boundary, and identifying what is explicitly outside that boundary. Ask the people who operate and consume it whether the description is distinct from neighboring capabilities before assigning a permanent ID.

Information type: Example. “Deployment metadata” can describe the structured product, task, and deployment context needed by downstream services. A separate “Contextual guidance” capability can describe the guidance presented to a user, while depending on deployment metadata and a content service. These names and relationships come from the sample and must be validated for the project.

docs.title: Gather evidence and rate maturity
docs.text:
Information type: Principle. A maturity rating should summarize demonstrated capability against a documented rubric, not the analyst’s impression of how advanced a team feels. For each proposed current and target rating, record the evidence, the person who validated it, the date, the assumptions, and any gap between actual practice and planned intent.

Information type: Procedure. Gather evidence from the people closest to the work and from artifacts that show the work is repeatable. Compare how the capability is defined, delivered, operated, measured, and improved; then agree which maturity-level description is supported today and which level is an achievable planning target.

Information type: Fact. The application ships with nine example maturity levels, numbered M0 through M8, and treats the last position as an open-ended wider-domain horizon. The labels and descriptions are defaults, not an approved industry standard; each capability can have its own editable level names and descriptions, and the level list can be expanded or reordered in the Journey.

Information type: Principle. Maturity 8+ means that the wider-domain horizon can continue to evolve; it is not a certification or a fixed maximum. Use levels that stakeholders can distinguish with observable evidence, and avoid assigning a level simply because it appears farther along the scale.

docs.title: Define ownership and dependencies
docs.text:
Information type: Concept. Ownership identifies who is responsible for delivering a capability at a point in the plan, while a handoff period identifies when responsibility is expected to change. A dependency identifies another capability that must support or enable the selected capability; it does not by itself assign ownership or prove that the dependency is ready.

Information type: Procedure. For every capability, identify the current owner, the intended future owner, the handoff period, and the decision or unresolved question behind that choice. Then list only direct dependencies by their stable IDs, and confirm that each dependency exists and is understood by both capability owners.

Information type: Fact. The built-in owner IDs are appliance and federated, although users can change their displayed names in Settings. The editor’s handoff period defaults to the end of the timeline; an explicitly entered handoff date changes which owner is shown from that period onward.

docs.title: Choose perspectives and timeline
docs.text:
Information type: Concept. An audience perspective is a lens for asking what a stakeholder needs to understand or decide about a capability. The default perspectives are client, consultant, product team, leadership, and wider domain; their labels, roles, and stated needs can be edited in Settings.

Information type: Fact. The timeline has a granularity of month, quarter, half-year, or year, a start date, and two to sixty periods. The asOf date anchors each capability’s current maturity value, while the final timeline period anchors its target value; dated milestones can describe intermediate or historical values.

Information type: Concept. The header’s Current and Focus controls select the two periods compared in the views, and either period can be before or after the other. Current is the reference date and Focus is the date being compared; neither control is a current/future switch, and changing them for an analysis does not rewrite the YAML asOf anchor.

Information type: Principle. A timeline should match the way the planning group makes commitments. Choose monthly detail only when decisions can be meaningfully made at that cadence; otherwise, use quarters, half-years, or years to avoid suggesting more precision than the evidence supports.

docs.title: 3. Prepare the YAML document
docs.text:
Information type: Structure. YAML is the canonical capability document that the application imports and exports. The exported format is a versioned object containing settings and a nonempty capabilities list; the application also accepts a bare list of capabilities, but the object form preserves the project settings and is the recommended format.

classDiagram
    class CapabilityDocument {
      +version: 1
      +settings: Settings
      +capabilities: Capability[]
    }
    class Settings {
      +ownerLabels: OwnerLabels
      +audiences: Audience[]
      +timeline: Timeline
    }
    class Capability {
      +id: string
      +name: string
      +summary: string
      +current: number
      +target: number
      +owner: appliance | federated
      +futureOwner: appliance | federated
      +handoffDate: ISO date
      +levels: Level[]
      +milestones: Milestone[]
      +dependencies: string[]
      +decision: string
      +dita: object
    }
    class Level {
      +name: string
      +description: string
    }
    class Milestone {
      +date: ISO date
      +maturity: number
    }
    CapabilityDocument *-- Settings
    CapabilityDocument *-- Capability
    Capability *-- Level
    Capability *-- Milestone
    Capability ..> Capability : depends on

Information type: Example. The following excerpt shows a capability with the principal planning fields. Use the complete YAML format reference for settings, levels, dates, and validation details.

version: 1
settings:
  ownerLabels:
    appliance: Appliance
    federated: Federated
  timeline:
    granularity: quarter
    start: 2026-10-01
    periods: 9
    asOf: 2026-10-01
  audiences:
    - id: client
      label: Client
      description: Uses and funds the capability
      need: Clear outcomes and a dependable operating experience.
capabilities:
  - id: contextual-guidance
    name: Contextual guidance
    summary: Relevant guidance at the point of need.
    current: 3
    target: 5
    owner: appliance
    futureOwner: federated
    handoffDate: 2028-10-01
    decision: Agree on the handoff to the shared content service.
    dependencies:
      - deployment-metadata
      - content-service
    levels:
      - name: Emerging
        description: Explore the need.
      - name: Initial
        description: Describe the capability.
      - name: Defined
        description: Define the model.
      - name: Managed
        description: Operate a first version.
      - name: Measured
        description: Measure outcomes.
      - name: Optimized
        description: Optimize the handoff.
    milestones:
      - date: 2027-10-01
        maturity: 4
    dita:
      audience:
        - client
      maturity: phase-3
      ownership: appliance-native

Information type: Procedure. Create a project copy of the bundled example, then replace its illustrative values instead of editing the only copy. Give each capability a unique, stable ID; write a concise name and summary; set current and target; specify both owners; add known dependencies; and record the rationale in decision.

Information type: Procedure. Add explicit levels when the project has an approved maturity rubric, because the editor and desktop validator use those definitions to interpret maturity values. Add milestones only when there is evidence or an agreed planning event at a date between the current anchor and target horizon; save dates as ISO YYYY-MM-DD values.

Information type: Procedure. Add settings when the project needs audience-specific wording, custom owner labels, or a different planning horizon. Keep the built-in owner IDs appliance and federated even when their visible labels are renamed, and make sure each audience has a stable id, label, role description, and stated need.

Information type: Principle. Treat the dita object as proposed content metadata, not as a validated CCMS configuration. Record only mapping hypotheses that the content team can review, and do not interpret the example’s audience, maturity, or ownership tags as approved filter rules.

docs.title: 4. Start the application and import data
Choose a runtime
docs.text:
Information type: Concept. The browser preview and the Tauri desktop app use the same planning interface but have different persistence and validation behavior. The browser keeps changes in memory until export and does not run the Python sidecar; the desktop app loads its saved YAML when present, validates changes with the sidecar, and saves successful changes in its application data directory.

Information type: Procedure. To run the browser preview, install the project dependencies and start Vite from the repository root.

npm install
npm run dev

Information type: Procedure. To run the Tauri app during development, build the Python sidecar and start the desktop shell. Python 3.10 or later, a virtual environment, and the platform prerequisites for Tauri 2 are required.

python3 -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
npm install
npm run sidecar:build
npm run tauri dev

Information type: Procedure. Import project data by choosing Import YAML in the application header and selecting a .yaml or .yml file. A successful import replaces the active capability set, selects the first capability in the file, and resets the comparison periods to the settings’ asOf date and the final timeline period.

Information type: Fact. A failed import reports an error and does not replace the active set. Desktop validation checks the capability list, maturity range and levels, and dependency references, but the importer normalizes missing or unrecognized owner values to appliance before validation; provide the IDs appliance or federated explicitly. Browser validation is weaker and does not check all cross-record relationships, so validate project files in the desktop app before relying on them.

docs.title: 5. Navigate the screens
docs.text:
Information type: Structure. The interface keeps one planning context across the three views: the selected capability, selected audience perspective, Current reference period, and Focus comparison period. The sidebar changes the view without resetting that context, while the header controls select the capability, perspective, timeline granularity, and comparison periods.

flowchart TB
    subgraph Shell["Application shell"]
      S["Sidebar: Matrix / Capability journey / Domain map"]
      H["Header: capability · perspective · granularity · Current · Focus"]
      A["Actions: Content mapping · Settings · Import YAML · Export YAML · Print report · Edit capability"]
      V["Active view"]
      S --> V
      H --> V
      A --> V
    end

docs.title: Matrix
docs.text:
Information type: Concept. The Matrix is the comparison screen for examining how capability reach and maturity relate to stakeholder perspectives. Its audience rows, maturity axis, capability bars, ownership legend, and selected-capability panel help frame a discussion; they do not replace evidence or stakeholder agreement.

flowchart LR
    subgraph Matrix["Matrix screen"]
      M1["Audience rows"]
      M2["Maturity axis and capability bars"]
      M3["Current and Focus markers"]
      M4["Legend: owner and planned reach"]
      M5["Selected capability panel: summary, need, dependencies, decision"]
      M6["Explore: Capability journey / Domain map"]
      M1 --- M2
      M2 --- M3
      M2 --- M4
      M2 --- M6
      M5 --- M2
    end

Information type: Procedure. To inspect a capability in the Matrix, choose it from the Selected capability control or select its bar. Choose an audience under Perspective, set Current and Focus to the dates you want to compare, and read the audience need, dependencies, ownership decision, and maturity markers in the adjacent panel.

Information type: Fact. Matrix bar placement is partly configured for the bundled sample, and imported data may not be represented as a complete, project-authored audience layout. Check that the relevant bars appear and make sense for your project before treating their placement as a planning conclusion.

docs.title: Capability journey
docs.text:
Information type: Concept. The Capability journey is the detail screen for one capability’s maturity definition and planned path. It combines maturity-level descriptions, the values at Current and Focus, an ownership ribbon, dependencies, audience impact lanes, and the scope decision.

flowchart LR
    subgraph Journey["Capability journey screen"]
      J1["Capability name, summary, scope decision"]
      J2["Maturity stages and descriptions"]
      J3["Current / Focus markers"]
      J4["Ownership ribbon"]
      J5["Dependencies"]
      J6["Audience impact"]
      J7["Define maturity levels"]
      J8["Manage dependencies"]
      J1 --> J2
      J2 --> J3
      J2 --> J7
      J1 --> J4
      J4 --> J5
      J5 --> J8
      J5 --> J6
    end

Information type: Procedure. To review the maturity path, choose a stage in the journey to read its description. Use Set as current or Set as target when the agreed rating changes; the application adjusts the corresponding maturity value and saves the record through the normal validation path.

Information type: Procedure. To revise the rubric for one capability, choose Define maturity levels, edit the level names or descriptions, reorder or remove levels, or add a level, then choose Save levels. Keep at least two named levels; when levels are reordered or removed, the editor remaps the capability’s current, target, and milestone values to the revised list.

Information type: Procedure. To revise relationships, choose Manage dependencies, add or remove the capabilities that this capability relies on, and choose Save dependencies. The dependency list is directional: the selected capability names its prerequisites, and the Domain map draws the relationship toward the capability that depends on them.

docs.title: Federated domain map
docs.text:
Information type: Concept. The Federated domain map is the relationship screen for tracing dependencies and discussing responsibility boundaries. Capability nodes show the owner at the Focus period, while dependency arrows connect prerequisites to dependent capabilities.

flowchart LR
    subgraph DomainMap["Federated domain map"]
      D1["Product / appliance zone"]
      D2["Responsibility boundary"]
      D3["Federated environment zone"]
      D4["Capability nodes with maturity and owner"]
      D5["Dependency arrows"]
      D6["Selected capability insight and handoff alert"]
      D7["Resolve ownership → Edit capability"]
      D1 --- D2 --- D3
      D4 --> D5
      D5 --> D6
      D6 --> D7
    end

Information type: Procedure. To trace a relationship, select a node and inspect the selected-capability panel for upstream dependencies, the current and future owner decision, and the maturity at Focus. Choose Resolve ownership to open the capability editor, clarify the decision with the relevant owners, and save the agreed change.

Information type: Fact. The map’s node positions are generated for the bundled capabilities and arranged heuristically for other records. Treat the map as a dependency and ownership discussion aid, not a formally governed architecture diagram.

docs.title: 6. Edit the project and its settings
Edit a capability
docs.text:
Information type: Procedure. To update a capability, choose Edit capability from any view, make the agreed changes, and choose Save changes. The editor covers the capability name, summary, current and target maturity, current and future owners, handoff period, scope decision, timeline milestones, and direct dependencies.

Information type: Fact. The graphical editor edits existing capability records; it does not create or delete capabilities. Prepare new capability records in the YAML before importing them, and remove a capability from the YAML only after updating every dependency that points to its ID.

Information type: Procedure. To represent an intermediate event or planned step, add a timeline milestone, select its date, and enter the maturity value that applies then. Current maturity is anchored at settings.timeline.asOf, target maturity is anchored at the final timeline period, and the application estimates intervening maturity by interpolating between dated points.

docs.title: Configure Settings
docs.text:
Information type: Procedure. Choose Settings to change the displayed names for the Appliance and Federated owners, edit or add audience perspectives, or set the timeline’s granularity, number of periods, start date, and asOf reference date. Choose Save settings to validate and apply the settings to the shared views.

Information type: Fact. Timeline granularity can be monthly, quarterly, biannual, or yearly, and the number of periods must be from two through sixty. Dates are stored as ISO strings, so changing the granularity changes period labels and the displayed span without changing the stored milestone dates.

Information type: Principle. Edit asOf only when the project’s definition of the current maturity anchor changes; use the header’s Current selector to compare a different reference period for an analysis. This distinction preserves the meaning of the source rating while still allowing the group to examine a different time slice.

docs.title: Review Content mapping
docs.text:
Information type: Concept. Content mapping is a read-only planning panel for proposed DITA audience, maturity, and ownership metadata on the selected capability. It can help a content analyst frame a conversation, but it does not validate the mapping against a content model.

Information type: Fact. The application does not publish embedded content, create production DITAVAL rules, call a CCMS Deploy API, or generate PDF manuals. Validate any proposed mapping with the content team before using it in a publishing process; CCMS deployment and PDF generation remain future integration targets.

docs.title: 7. Use the matrix to make and communicate a plan
docs.text:
Information type: Process. A planning conversation should move from comparison to explanation to relationship testing before stakeholders settle on an action. The shared selection lets participants examine the same capability from multiple views without losing the audience or periods under discussion.

sequenceDiagram
    actor Analyst
    participant Matrix
    participant Journey
    participant Map as Domain map
    participant YAML as Project YAML
    Analyst->>Matrix: Select audience, capability, Current, and Focus
    Matrix-->>Analyst: Compare maturity and audience need
    Analyst->>Journey: Inspect stages, owners, and milestones
    Journey-->>Analyst: Review evidence, gap, and target
    Analyst->>Map: Trace dependencies and boundary
    Map-->>Analyst: Identify handoff and upstream owners
    Analyst->>Journey: Edit decision, maturity, or dependencies
    Journey->>YAML: Save validated planning record
    Analyst->>YAML: Export reviewed snapshot

Information type: Procedure. Begin the meeting with one agreed capability and audience, then choose a Current reference period and a Focus period that matches the planning question. In the Matrix, state the evidence behind the current maturity and explain whose need the target is intended to meet.

Information type: Procedure. Continue in the Journey by comparing the maturity descriptions at the two periods, reviewing each milestone, and testing whether the proposed target is supported by a feasible sequence of work. Use the level descriptions to expose disagreement about what “ready” or “managed” means instead of averaging incompatible judgments.

Information type: Procedure. Continue in the Domain map by tracing each prerequisite to its owner and checking whether the proposed handoff leaves an unowned responsibility. Record the agreed owner, handoff period, dependency, or unresolved decision in the capability editor, and obtain confirmation from the affected owners.

Information type: Principle. Treat the result as a versioned planning snapshot, not as proof that future work has happened. Keep the evidence and approval record with the project’s normal decision artifacts, and update the YAML only when the responsible people agree that the plan or its supporting facts have changed.

docs.title: 8. Save, export, and reuse data
docs.text:
Information type: Concept. Exported YAML is the portable project artifact that preserves capability records and settings for reuse. The printed view is a meeting aid for the active screen, while the YAML is the structured source needed to continue editing, compare versions, or transfer the planning model.

Information type: Procedure. Choose Export YAML to download the current document as capability-ownership.yaml. Save that file in the project’s approved repository or document store, include the review date and decision context in the surrounding project record, and use the exported file as the starting point for the next cycle.

Information type: Fact. In the browser preview, edits remain in memory until exported and are lost if the page is refreshed or closed first. In the desktop app, successful imports, capability edits, and settings changes are saved to the Tauri app data file named capabilities.yaml; export remains useful for backup, review, and transfer.

Information type: Procedure. Choose Print report when stakeholders need a paper or PDF copy of the active view. The desktop app invokes the Tauri print command; the browser preview invokes the browser’s print dialog. Set the capability, perspective, timeline, and active view before printing because the control prints the current view, not a combined report of all three screens.

Information type: Principle. Use the exported file as the controlled source for handoffs between analysts and as the input to later planning cycles. Review diffs between exports so changes to maturity, ownership, dependencies, audience definitions, and timeline settings are deliberate and traceable.

docs.title: 9. Troubleshooting and guardrails
docs.text:
Information type: Troubleshooting. If an import fails, confirm that the file parses as YAML and contains a nonempty capabilities list, then check that every record has a unique nonempty ID, a name, and nonnegative numeric maturity values. In the desktop app, also check that the target is not below current, maturity values fit the levels, owners use the IDs appliance or federated, and every dependency points to another record without a self-reference.

Information type: Troubleshooting. If a change appears in the browser but disappears after reopening the page, export the YAML before closing or refreshing; the browser does not save automatically. If the desktop app cannot load or save its document, read the error notification and check that the application can access its Tauri app data directory.

Information type: Troubleshooting. If a capability or audience is missing from a view, confirm that the record is in the imported file, that the intended audience is selected, and that the relevant relationship or audience metadata exists. Matrix placement is partly sample-configured, and Journey audience-impact lanes are illustrative for the built-in perspectives, so verify those visual summaries against project evidence.

Information type: Troubleshooting. If a dependency is absent from the Domain map, check that the selected capability lists the prerequisite’s exact ID and that the prerequisite is present in the same document. A browser import may not report all broken relationships because the browser preview does not run the Python sidecar; use desktop validation for a relationship check.

Information type: Guardrail. Do not describe the example data as client-approved, the DITA panel as a validated CCMS configuration, a printed view as a generated PDF manual, or a visual dependency as an approved architecture decision. Each of those claims requires review and evidence outside the current prototype.

docs.title: 10. Related reference
docs.text: Information type: Reference. The YAML format reference defines document fields, accepted values, and validation differences between runtimes. The project README covers installation, desktop development, and documentation commands.

docs.title: YAML format reference
docs.text: YAML is the canonical capability document used by the Capability and Ownership Matrix. This reference describes the recommended exported document, field meanings, and the differences between browser and desktop validation; use it with the analyst user guide when preparing or reviewing project data.

docs.title: Document shape
docs.text:
The recommended document is a YAML object with version, settings, and a nonempty capabilities list. The importer also accepts a bare list of capability records, but a bare list cannot preserve project settings when exported.

version: 1
settings:
  ownerLabels:
    appliance: Appliance
    federated: Federated
  timeline:
    granularity: quarter
    start: 2026-10-01
    periods: 9
    asOf: 2026-10-01
  audiences:
    - id: client
      label: Client
      description: Uses and funds the capability
      need: Clear outcomes and a dependable operating experience.
capabilities:
  - id: contextual-guidance
    name: Contextual guidance
    summary: Relevant guidance at the point of need.
    current: 3
    target: 5
    owner: appliance
    futureOwner: federated
    handoffDate: 2028-10-01
    decision: Agree on the handoff to a shared content service.
    dependencies:
      - deployment-metadata
      - content-service
    levels:
      - name: Emerging
        description: Explore the need.
      - name: Initial
        description: Describe the capability.
      - name: Defined
        description: Define the model.
      - name: Managed
        description: Operate a first version.
      - name: Measured
        description: Measure outcomes.
    milestones:
      - date: 2027-10-01
        maturity: 4
    dita:
      audience: [client, consultant]
      maturity: phase-3
      ownership: appliance-native

The bundled capabilities.yaml contains six illustrative capabilities and project settings. Its capability facts, IDs, maturity values, dependencies, audience wording, and DITA metadata are examples, not an approved project model.

docs.title: Document and settings fields
docs.text:
Field Required in source Meaning version Recommended Exported as 1. The current importer does not reject an unsupported or missing version; version migration is not implemented. settings Optional Project-wide owner labels, audience perspectives, and timeline. Missing settings are replaced with defaults. settings.ownerLabels.appliance Optional Display label for owner ID appliance; defaults to Appliance. settings.ownerLabels.federated Optional Display label for owner ID federated; defaults to Federated. settings.audiences Optional List of audience perspectives. Each item has id, label, description, and need. If omitted, the five built-in perspectives are used. settings.timeline.granularity Optional Period unit: month, quarter, biannual, or year. The default is quarter. settings.timeline.start Optional ISO date (YYYY-MM-DD) for the first period; defaults to 2026-10-01. settings.timeline.periods Optional Number of periods, from 2 through 60; defaults to 9. settings.timeline.asOf Optional ISO date that anchors each capability’s current maturity; defaults to the timeline start.

Audience IDs should be stable, nonempty identifiers, and the label, role description, and need should be understandable to the planning group. The built-in IDs are client, consultant, product-team, leadership, and wider-domain; custom IDs can be used, but some Journey audience-impact text is illustrative for the built-in set.

Timeline dates should be valid calendar dates in ISO form. The start date, granularity, and period count define the timeline; changing the granularity changes the period labels and span, while milestone dates remain ISO dates.

docs.title: Capability fields
docs.text:
Field Required in source Meaning and guidance id Yes Unique, nonempty, stable identifier. Other records refer to it from dependencies. Avoid changing it when only the display name changes. name Yes Nonempty display name for the capability. summary Recommended Short description of the ability or outcome; defaults to an empty string when omitted. current Yes Nonnegative numeric maturity value. It is anchored at settings.timeline.asOf. target Yes Nonnegative numeric maturity value planned for the final timeline period. Desktop validation requires it to be at least current. owner Yes Current owner ID: appliance or federated. futureOwner Yes Planned owner ID: appliance or federated. handoffDate Optional ISO date when the future owner takes responsibility. If omitted, the owner changes at the last timeline period. decision Recommended Scope, ownership, or planning rationale to discuss with stakeholders; defaults to an empty string. dependencies Recommended List of IDs of other capabilities this capability relies on. Use [] for none. levels Recommended Ordered maturity-level definitions for this capability; each item has a nonempty name and optional description. milestones Optional Dated maturity points between or outside the current and target anchors; each item has an ISO date and numeric maturity. dita Optional Proposed DITA/content metadata. Values are planning notes, not validated publishing configuration.

Maturity values are numeric and correspond to positions in the capability’s ordered levels list, starting at zero. The editor supports at least two levels and up to twenty levels. Desktop validation checks that current, target, and milestone maturity values do not exceed the highest level, and it checks that target is not below current; use whole numbers that match the ordered levels.

If levels is omitted or empty, the application supplies default maturity-level names and descriptions. Explicit level definitions are recommended for project data because they make the rubric portable and visible in exported YAML.

The model estimates maturity at selected dates by interpolating between the asOf current value, dated milestones, and the target at the end of the timeline. The selected Current and Focus periods are view controls; they do not overwrite these stored anchors.

docs.title: Ownership and dependencies
docs.text:
Ownership uses fixed IDs and editable labels. Use appliance for the product-side owner and federated for the wider-environment owner; changing the display labels in settings does not change those IDs.

Each dependency must refer to a capability ID in the same document. A record cannot depend on itself, and desktop validation rejects missing dependency IDs; the validator does not check dependency cycles or determine whether an upstream capability is ready.

flowchart LR
    A["deployment-metadata"] -->|"prerequisite for"| B["content-service"]
    B -->|"prerequisite for"| C["contextual-guidance"]

In the YAML, the dependent record contains the IDs of its prerequisites. For example, contextual-guidance lists content-service in its own dependencies array, while the diagram draws the arrow from the prerequisite to the dependent capability.

docs.title: DITA planning metadata
docs.text:
The optional dita value is an object for proposed content annotations. The bundled example uses audience, maturity, and ownership, but the current app does not validate those values against a DITA content model.

Do not treat these fields as approved DITA attributes, production DITAVAL filters, or a validated CCMS configuration. The tool does not call the CCMS, deploy embedded content, or generate PDF manuals; validate all proposed mappings with the content team before using them in a publishing workflow.

docs.title: Validation behavior
docs.text:
The React importer requires a nonempty capability list, unique nonempty IDs, nonempty names, and nonnegative numeric current and target values. It normalizes omitted optional fields and unknown owner IDs; do not rely on those defaults for project data.

In the Tauri desktop app, the Python sidecar additionally checks that targets are not below current values, levels contain at least two named entries, maturity values fit the level list, owner IDs are valid, and dependencies refer to existing IDs without self-reference. However, the React importer normalizes missing or unrecognized owner values to appliance before the sidecar receives them, so an owner typo may not be reported as an error. Supply appliance or federated explicitly. A failed import or edit is reported and the active document remains unchanged.

The browser preview does not run the sidecar and does not provide equivalent cross-record validation. It does not reject a target below current maturity or a missing dependency reference, and it normalizes unknown owner IDs to appliance; these values can produce misleading planning data. Validate the YAML in the desktop app before using the browser preview for planning.

The current importer does not enforce the version value, reject dependency cycles, verify that audience IDs in DITA metadata exist in settings, or validate DITA attributes. Treat these as analyst review responsibilities.

docs.title: Prepare and import a file
docs.text:
Create a project copy of the sample, replace all illustrative records, preserve stable IDs, and check every dependency after editing or removing capabilities. Keep the project’s maturity rubric and audience descriptions alongside the YAML so reviewers can understand the values rather than infer their meaning from the chart.

Save the file with a .yaml or .yml extension, then choose Import YAML in the application. Desktop validation is recommended before the first planning review; after changes in either runtime, choose Export YAML to create capability-ownership.yaml and keep that exported version in the project’s approved document store.
